title: Free if you take yourself as free
hookLine: one verse says the one who takes themselves to be free is free, and the one who takes themselves to be bound is bound
carry: not the doer: the binding lives in the taking
tomorrow: Aho: the wave finds it is water

lines: FREE, IF YOU TAKE YOURSELF AS FREE.
cards: Free, if you take yourself as free. Bound, if you take yourself as bound. That's the line, in paraphrase, from the first chapter of the Ashtavakra Gita.

And the sage doesn't call it his own discovery. He says it's a saying people repeat, and the saying is true: as the mind holds itself, so it goes. A strange thing to hear on the thousandth day of anything.
A thousand days could feel like finally getting somewhere, or like miles still to go. This verse quietly asks about both: who is doing the counting?

teach.h: NOT A POSTER ON A GYM WALL.
teach.b: Read quickly, the verse sounds like a poster on a gym wall: believe in yourself and anything is possible. The verses around it show it means something stranger.
A few verses earlier, the sage tells Janaka that bondage is this one thing: seeing someone else as the seer, rather than yourself.

teach.h: BITTEN BY THE SNAKE OF I AM THE DOER.
teach.b: He says the king has been bitten by the black snake of egoism, the thought, I am the doer.

Hindu teachers call that ahamkara, the I-maker, and the Bhagavad Gita says the same: the one deluded by ego thinks, I am the doer. Drink the nectar of faith in the thought, I am not the doer, he says, and be happy.
Then comes the line: one who holds that they're free is free; one who holds that they're bound is bound. So it isn't positive thinking, think hard enough and life gets better.

teach.h: THE BINDING WAS IN THE TAKING.
teach.b: It says the binding was never in the world. It was in the taking, in what consciousness took itself to be.
Ashtavakra's word for free is mukta. On his account, nobody builds their way to mukta. They stop insisting they're bound.
A thousand days in, that cuts both ways. The days of practice are real: the sitting, the lamps, the songs. But this book would say the one who sat for all of them was never in a cell.
Freedom, on its account, isn't a reward at the end of a long climb.
It's a fact about the climber, there on day one, and on day one thousand.

how: Students of the Ashtavakra Gita often memorize or recite individual verses in Sanskrit, and the verse on being free or bound is one that teachers quote when discussing how bondage, on this view, lies in identification rather than in the world.

o: a vow taken when someone leaves home for good
a mind trained to think only happy thoughts
free: no longer taking yourself as bound

games.q: free or bound — tap the pairs.
p: the thought, I am the doer
the thought, I am not the doer
seeing someone else as the seer

s: the verse means positive thinking will get you a better life
it says the binding was in what consciousness took itself to be, not in the world.
the sage calls the line a saying people repeat, and says it is true
he presents it as a common saying, and affirms it.
on this account, freedom is a reward at the end of long practice
the book treats it as a fact about the one practicing, there on day one.

games.q: you're Janaka. the sage says you've been bitten by a black snake. what is the snake?
o: a curse from a rival king.
the thought, I am the doer.
games.why: the snake is egoism, the thought I am the doer; the cure is the nectar of faith in the thought I am not the doer.

practice: Notice the sense of being the one doing all this: sitting, breathing, trying. Then try the sage's small turn: let the breath breathe itself, and let sounds arrive without anyone needing to hear them.

If the thought I'm doing this comes back, notice it as one more thought passing through. If you pray, end the way many Hindus end a task or a meal: Shri Krishnarpanamastu, may this be offered to Krishna.

wordCard.voice: Mukta. Free, released. In the Ashtavakra Gita, free if you take yourself as free, bound if you take yourself as bound.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: mukta, free, released. The word for free in this verse.

carryVoice: Your line: not the doer, the binding lives in the taking. A thousand days in, the sage would only ask who is counting. Day one thousand.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 3.27 (the one deluded by ego thinks, I am the doer)
